newsitem.title: CHINA: Families mourn 86 killed in China mine blasts.
newsitem.headline: Families mourn 86 killed in China mine blasts.

text.p: A series of explosions that ripped through three privately-run coal mines in central China last week killed 86 miners and left three fighting for life, officials said on Tuesday.

Local guesthouses were filled by family members who came to mourn relatives killed last Tuesday while labouring at pit faces in Pingdingshan county in the central province of Henan, the officials said.

The blasts, which were caused by gas in the connected mine shafts, killed all but 12 of the 98 men caught underground in the three mines and left three of the survivors fighting for life in hospital, coal bureau officials said.
"One of the three is still in a coma and his situation is very serious. The explosion ripped open his windpipe," said a doctor at the Pingdingshan Mine District Hospital.
Officials said the explosions occurred in three separately operated, privately-run mines. One of the mines had two shafts and the others one each, but all were connected below the surface.
"There are old tunnels underground that link the four shafts and when an explosion happened in one it set off blasts in the others," said one local official.
Another official said the mine managers had been taken into custody for questioning by investigators from the central government.
"The county guesthouses are filled with relatives of the miners," said a town government worker.
A local government department set up to handle the disaster had been doling out compensation to relatives of dead miners from other provinces. Many had already returned to their homes, he said.

The tragedy in Pingdingshan county, about 760 km (460 miles) south of Beijing, was the latest in a long list of disasters suffered by China's huge army of miners, many of whom toil in badly maintained and poorly regulated pits.
Explosions and other accidents kill up to 10,000 miners a year, with coal mines accounting for more than a third of the toll, government statistics show.
Beijing in February vowed to sack the managers of coal mines which suffered serious accidents and to launch reforms to boost safety, efficiency and economic returns.
State media have reported that nearly 25 percent of coal mine accidents happen at unlicensed mines, saying poor management and neglect of mining safety laws are to blame for many disasters.
